posts.author: Mara Ellison
posts.title: The quiet return of the dedicated music player
posts.excerpt: Phones do everything, which is exactly why a growing number of people are buying a device that only plays music — and keeping it in a drawer by the door.
body: Phones do everything, which is exactly why a growing number of people are buying a device that only plays music.
The appeal is not the sound, though the sound is often better. It is the absence of everything else: no messages arriving between songs, no feed waiting one swipe away.
Most of the people we spoke to described the same moment. They reached for the phone to change a track, and twenty minutes later they were still holding it, the album long finished.

A player with a small screen and a few buttons does one thing and then gets out of the way. Some are new, built around files you copy over by hand; others are ten-year-old models bought second-hand and given a fresh battery.
None of this needs a new habit. It needs a small change to the one you already have, made on a quiet afternoon and then left alone for a few weeks so you can see whether it holds.
The details matter less than the direction. Try it once as described, note what felt awkward, and adjust a single thing at a time. Most of the gain comes from the first attempt anyway.

posts.author: Owen Hartley
posts.title: Why your laptop battery report says 80 percent and what that really means
posts.excerpt: Battery health numbers are estimates built on a model of the cell. Here is how the model works, and when the number is worth worrying about.
body: Battery health numbers are estimates built on a model of the cell, not a measurement of it.
The firmware tracks how much charge goes in and comes out, and compares it with what the cell held when new. Temperature, age and how often the battery sits at full all move the estimate.
A reading of 80 percent after three years is normal. A sudden drop of ten points in a month is not, and is worth a closer look.

posts.author: Lena Ortiz
posts.title: Weeknight braised beans that taste like they took all day
posts.excerpt: A pot of beans, a few aromatics and one trick with the cooking liquid. Forty minutes, most of it hands-off.
body: A pot of beans, a few aromatics and one trick with the cooking liquid: reduce half of it hard in a separate pan, then stir it back in.
The reduction concentrates everything that makes slow-cooked beans taste the way they do, in a fraction of the time.

posts.author: Priya Raman
posts.title: Designing forms that forgive: error states people understand
posts.excerpt: Most form errors blame the person. A few patterns — inline hints, kept input, specific messages — turn them into help instead.
body: Most form errors blame the person filling in the form. They arrive late, after the button, in red, and say what went wrong without saying what to do.
Three patterns change that: hints that appear while typing, input that survives a failed submit, and messages that name the fix rather than the fault.

posts.author: Nadia Brooks
posts.title: The long tail of a single typo in a config file
posts.excerpt: A misplaced character took a service down for six hours. The postmortem is a quiet masterclass in how small things travel.
body: A misplaced character took a service down for six hours. The postmortem is a quiet masterclass in how small things travel through big systems.
Nothing in the chain was unusual. Each step trusted the one before it, as it should, and the typo passed through all of them.

posts.author: Sam Whitaker
posts.title: The best way to store herbs so they last a week
posts.excerpt: Treat soft herbs like flowers and hard herbs like vegetables. We tested six methods over ten days.
body: Treat soft herbs like flowers and hard herbs like vegetables. We tested six methods over ten days, and two came out clearly ahead.
Parsley, cilantro and mint did best upright in a jar of water in the fridge, loosely covered. Rosemary and thyme lasted longest wrapped in a barely damp towel.

posts.author: Tomás Herrera
posts.title: A practical guide to container queries in real layouts
posts.excerpt: Components that adapt to their own space, not the window's. What works today, and what to keep a fallback for.
body: Container queries let a component adapt to the space it is given, not to the size of the window.
That sounds like a small change. In practice it removes a whole category of special cases: the card that looks right in the main column and wrong in the sidebar.

posts.author: Owen Hartley
posts.title: How a tiny satellite keeps its antenna pointed home
posts.excerpt: Reaction wheels, magnetorquers and a lot of patience: the attitude control of a shoebox-sized spacecraft.
body: Reaction wheels, magnetorquers and a lot of patience keep a shoebox-sized spacecraft pointed where it needs to be.
The wheels spin up to turn the satellite the other way. Over time they saturate, and small electromagnets push against the Earth's field to bleed the momentum off.

posts.author: Lena Ortiz
posts.title: Crisp roast potatoes, every time
posts.excerpt: Parboil, rough them up, then roast hot. The baking soda in the water is the part people skip.
body: Parboil, rough them up, then roast hot. The pinch of baking soda in the water is the part people skip, and it is the part that matters.
It breaks down the surface just enough to make a starchy paste, which fries into a crust in the oven.

posts.title: Motion that helps: when to animate an interface
posts.excerpt: Animation should explain a change, not decorate it. A short checklist for deciding when it earns its place.
body: Animation should explain a change, not decorate it. If the person would lose track of where something went, show it moving; otherwise, let it appear.
